title: Marathon Training Plan for Beginners (18 Weeks)
excerpt: A complete first marathon schedule in miles and km: 4 runs a week, walk breaks allowed. Starts at 12-15 mi (19-24 km) a week and peaks at 35 mi (56 km).
body:
Marathon Training Plan for Beginners (18 Weeks)

This marathon training plan for beginners takes a first-time marathoner from about 12–15 miles (19–24 km) a week to the finish line in 18 weeks. You run four days a week, and walk breaks are allowed. Below is the complete week-by-week schedule in miles and kilometres, an effort-based pace key, and what to do when life gets in the way.

Weekly mileage peaks at 35 miles (56 km), and the longest run is 20 miles (32 km), three weeks before the race. Comparing options? Not sure which plan? Compare them here.

Who this plan is for

  • You are training for your first marathon.
  • You currently run about three times a week, 12–15 miles (19–24 km) in total, and can run 4–5 miles (6–8 km) without stopping.
  • You have 18 weeks until race day.
  • You don't have a time goal yet, or your goal is simply to finish strong.

Are you running less than that, or starting from scratch? Use the 6 month plan, which starts at 10–15 miles a week and adds six extra weeks of base building. If you can only run three days a week, the 3 day a week plan replaces the fourth run with cross-training.

The full 18-week beginner schedule (miles & km)

The plan has four runs a week: Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, with optional easy cross-training on Wednesday. Thursday starts as an easy run with strides. From week 6 it includes a few minutes of comfortably hard running, and in the last weeks it includes a little goal-pace running. Every other run is easy.

Pace key

  • Easy: conversational. You can speak in full sentences. If you have a goal time, about 90–120 s/mi (55–75 s/km) slower than goal pace. Walk breaks are fine.
  • Long run: the same easy effort. Run-walk (for example, 4 min running and 1 min walking) is welcome.
  • T (threshold): comfortably hard. You can say a few words at a time. About 30–45 s/mi (20–28 s/km) faster than goal pace. Jog 2–3 min between reps.
  • Goal pace: your realistic marathon pace (see "Setting a goal pace" below).
  • Strides: 20 s quick and relaxed at the end of an easy run. Walk back to recover.
  • Cross-train: optional easy cycling, swimming or elliptical. It doesn't count toward mileage.

How the plan is built

Weeks 1–5 build the habit. Mileage rises from 13 to 17 miles (21 to 27 km), and the long run moves from 5 to 7 miles (8 to 11 km). Weeks 6–12 add short threshold sessions on Thursdays and take the long run to 14 miles (23 km). Weeks 13–15 are the peak: long runs of 15, 17 and 20 miles (24, 27 and 32 km). Weeks 16–18 are the taper.

Every fourth week (weeks 4, 8 and 12) is a cutback week with about 20–25% less running. These weeks aren't optional. They are when your legs, tendons and bones adapt to the work. Weekly mileage never rises by more than about 15%, and most weeks rise by less than 10%.

How to adjust the plan

  • Run-walk: using a ratio such as 4 minutes running and 1 minute walking on long runs is a legitimate strategy, not a failure. Use the same ratio on race day.
  • Days: any four days work, as long as the long run isn't the day after Thursday's harder run.
  • Your race is 16 weeks away: start at week 3. If it is 20–24 weeks away, repeat weeks 1–4 or switch to the 6 month plan.
  • Missed runs: skip them and carry on. If you miss a long run, do the next scheduled one, but no more than 2 miles (3 km) longer than your last completed long run.
  • Pain or injury: pain that changes how you run, or doesn't ease within a few days, means stop and see a doctor or physio. Don't run through it.

Setting a goal pace

From week 13, Thursday includes a few miles at "goal pace". If you have raced a half marathon recently, double that time and add 15–20 minutes to get a realistic first-marathon goal, then use that pace. If you haven't raced, use the effort you could hold for 3–4 hours: slightly faster than your long runs, but still conversational in short sentences.

Fueling, strength and race week

Once your long runs pass 90 minutes, take a gel or sports drink every 30–40 minutes, so your stomach is used to it by race day. Two 20-minute strength sessions a week (squats, lunges, calf raises, planks) make the training easier to absorb. In race week, cut back, sleep, and eat a little more carbohydrate. Our guide to what a marathon plan should include covers each of these in detail.

FAQ

How long does it take to train for a first marathon?

Most beginners need 16–20 weeks if they can already run 4–5 miles comfortably. This plan uses 18 weeks. Starting from little or no running, allow about six months; see the 6 month plan.

How many days a week should a beginner run for a marathon?

Three or four. This plan uses four short-to-medium runs plus one long run within those four days. Five or more days isn't necessary for a first marathon and raises injury risk for newer runners.

Can I walk during a beginner marathon plan?

Yes. Planned walk breaks on long runs and on race day are a proven way for first-timers to finish feeling better. What matters is the total time on your feet each week, not running without stopping.

What pace should a beginner run long runs at?

Run at a conversational pace, where you can speak in full sentences. For most beginners that is 1–2 minutes per mile (40–75 seconds per km) slower than their eventual race pace. Running long runs too fast is the most common reason beginners get hurt.
keyTakeaway: A first marathon needs only four runs a week: build gradually from 13 to 35 miles, cut back every fourth week, and keep almost every run conversational.
